candidates.attack_scenario: Two independently authenticated clients (Client A and Client B) interact with the same A2A server. Client A creates a task. Client B, possessing valid credentials for the same server (e.g., a different authorized agent), learns or guesses Client A's task ID. Client B then uses standard protocol operations — GetTask to read Client A's task state and artifacts, CancelTask to terminate Client A's task, SubscribeToTask to receive Client A's real-time streaming updates, or CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig to redirect Client A's task notifications to Client B's own webhook. The protocol defines all task operations keyed solely by task ID. The Task data structure contains no owner or creator identity field. No session-to-task binding, task-scoped access token, or ownership proof mechanism exists at the protocol level. Authorization is vaguely delegated to implementations ('implementation-specific and MAY consider') with no interoperable protocol mechanism. The spec says 'Implementations MUST implement appropriate authorization scoping' for ListTasks, but 'appropriate' is undefined and no protocol-level mechanism (ownership field, binding token) is provided for any task operation. Different servers will invent incompatible authorization schemes, and clients have no protocol-level way to understand or interact with authorization controls. Even under full compliance with all normative requirements, the protocol provides no mechanism for the server to determine task ownership — that determination is entirely outside the protocol.

The PushNotificationConfig.authentication field (which specifies how the server authenticates TO the webhook) is optional — if omitted, the server sends unauthenticated POST requests to arbitrary public URLs. structural_observations: Agent card signing is explicitly optional (MAY) per the normative spec ('Agent Cards MAY be signed using JSON Web Signatures'). Client verification is SHOULD-level ('Clients SHOULD verify signatures when present'). When signing is not used — which is fully compliant — the only integrity guarantee for agent card content comes from TLS transport security. This means agent card authenticity is dependent solely on the trust relationship with the serving domain, with no content-level integrity protection. While this is an intentional design choice (MAY), it means agent card content used for security-critical decisions (service endpoint URL, securitySchemes) has no protocol-level tamper protection beyond TLS.

The protocol defines multi-agent authorization delegation via TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED bubbling ('An A2A client that is also an A2A agent SHOULD bubble up the TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED state to its own client') but provides no mechanism for provenance tracking of delegated credentials through multi-agent chains. In a chain A→B→C, when C requests auth and B delegates to A, the credential that eventually reaches C has no protocol-level provenance — C cannot verify through what path or how many intermediaries the credential traveled. This is partially mitigated by the spec's explicit delegation of credential acquisition to out-of-band processes.

The protocol defines no requirements for task ID format, entropy, or namespace isolation. Task IDs are client-provided opaque strings with no minimum entropy requirement. In the absence of protocol-level task-to-identity binding (C-001), the unguessability of task IDs becomes the de facto access control — yet the protocol imposes no constraints on task ID generation. Sequential, predictable, or low-entropy task IDs would significantly amplify the C-001 vulnerability.

The protocol explicitly states 'A2A protocol payloads, such as JSON-RPC messages, don't carry user or client identity information directly. Identity is established at the transport/HTTP layer.' This design means there is no in-band identity context that could be used for protocol-level authorization decisions across the task lifecycle. Combined with the absence of task-to-identity binding, this creates a fundamental gap where authentication (transport layer) and authorization (task layer) operate in disconnected layers with no protocol-defined bridge.

The A2A project roadmap explicitly lists 'Formalize inclusion of authorization schemes and optional credentials directly within the AgentCard' as a planned improvement, indicating the protocol designers are aware of the authorization mechanism gap but have not yet addressed it in the specification.
